analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal law requiring locally prevailing wages on federally funded construction projects.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon Act, backed by 123 House members, died in committee without ever getting a House floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out the Davis-Bacon Act of 1931, which requires that workers on federally financed construction projects be paid the locally prevailing wage for their trade. It would also repeal the Copeland Act, which makes the Labor Department enforce wage and payroll reporting rules on those contractors. Supporters said this would cut federal construction costs; the practical effect would be lower pay for the tradespeople who build federal buildings and highways.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction contractors bidding on federal projects gain the most: they could pay below the local prevailing wage, cutting their biggest cost. Taxpayers would save if bids actually came in lower, though how much is disputed — with cheaper labor, contractors can still keep the difference in their bids. Nonunion contractors that already pay below union scale would compete far more easily for federal work.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the requirement that contractors on federally financed or assisted construction pay the locally prevailing wage for each trade, letting them pay whatever the market allows on those jobs.

Repeals the Copeland Act, which requires the Secretary of Labor to regulate federal construction contractors and subcontractors — eliminating federal wage-enforcement oversight and certified payroll reporting on those projects.
Supporters' stated purpose was to lower the labor cost of federal construction; the bill takes effect 30 days after enactment but leaves existing contracts and outstanding bid invitations untouched.

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers — laborers and mechanics on federal projects — would see their pay fall from the locally prevailing rate to whatever their employer offers. Unionized building-trades workers, whose contract rates typically set the prevailing wage, would lose the most, and local contractors who pay union scale would face cheaper out-of-town competition.

drawbacks.text: Workers on federally funded buildings and public works would lose the wage floor that has required local prevailing pay since 1931, directly cutting take-home pay for the tradespeople the law covers.
Repealing the Copeland Act at the same time eliminates federal wage-enforcement and payroll reporting rules for these contractors, making underpayment of workers harder to detect.

Taxpayer savings are not guaranteed: with the wage floor gone, contractors could pocket the labor savings rather than pass them through in lower bids, so the public could end up with lower wages on federal jobs without lower prices.
Repeal would take effect just 30 days after enactment, leaving workers and contractors little time to adjust on new bids.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential taxpayer savings from cheaper bids are speculative, while the cost to workers is direct and certain: a repeal of the one wage floor on federal construction. For ordinary working people the trade is poor — pay falls first and price savings may never arrive.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared a House subcommittee but the full committee never approved it, so the bill sat there until the Congress ended in January 1997 without a floor vote.

narrative.text: Cass Ballenger introduced the bill on January 13, 1995, with 47 original cosponsors including top House Republican leaders Dick Armey and Tom DeLay, and it was referred to the Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities.
The bill eventually drew 123 cosponsors — 120 Republicans and 3 Democrats — about half the House Republican conference, showing substantial majority-party support for repeal.

In February 1995 the House asked the Labor Department for its comments, and on March 2, 1995 the Workforce Protections subcommittee held a markup and forwarded an amended version to the full committee.
The full Education and Workforce Committee never acted; there is no further action in the record after March 2, 1995, and the bill expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers and the building-trades unions that depend on prevailing-wage rates came out ahead, because the wage floor on federal projects stayed on the books. Contractors never got the right to pay below local prevailing wages on federal work.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 120 of the 123 cosponsors were Republicans, with only 3 Democrats, in a House run by a Republican majority that had made regulatory cuts a priority.

industries.note: Repeal would free contractors on federal jobs from paying the locally prevailing wage and from Labor Department payroll rules, cutting their labor costs. Any savings passed to taxpayers would come directly out of workers' paychecks, and any savings kept would be profit at the public's expense.
Union scale typically anchors the prevailing wage, so repeal would remove the main lever keeping federal construction pay at union rates and undercut union contractors' bids.
Firms that pay below prevailing rates could suddenly compete for federal work on equal terms, gaining market share while pushing down area wage standards.
